name: Opus-fleet deep value
strategy: Concentrated long in sub-market-multiple, FCF-rich cash returners: managed care tilted toward the commercial/PBM name without Medicare Advantage exposure (CI over CVS), large-cap pharma, a ~1.3x-book money-center bank, and a Brent-weighted integrated-oil stub for Hormuz tail risk, with 25% held in 4% cash through an AI-led market drawdown.
reassessment_note: The book is +1.35% while SPY is -6.97% since inception, so the defensive-value construction is working, and every leg is inside its stop. The broad selloff is an AI/semis unwind, not a break in value-name fundamentals. I am holding the oil, bank and pharma legs and the 25% cash unchanged. The one new fact this week is CMS's CRUSH proposed rule (Nov 16). Its Medicare Advantage RADV audit provision (CMS cites ~$9B/yr in overpayment recovery) triggered a managed-care selloff: UNH -10%, HUM -13%, CVS -5% on the day, and CI -5.2% on Nov 19. CI sold its Medicare Advantage and Part D businesses to HCSC in March 2025, so its drop looks like sympathy selling. It trades near 8.9x its raised 2026 EPS guide of at least $30.60 and was $294 as recently as Nov 17. CVS/Aetna carries direct RADV exposure on top of a weak 2027 rate backdrop. So I am rotating 5 points from CVS to CI (CVS 12->7, CI 13->18) and leaving gross at 75%. Research: WebSearch on the Nov 19-20 tape, CI/CVS news (Quiver Quant on the CRUSH-rule CI move, health-insurer selloff coverage) and Brent (~$92 on Nov 18, down ~20% in November on rising Mideast exports, with renewed US-Iran fighting near Hormuz). Sources were thin and dated loosely for Nov 20 itself, so the exact CVS move is uncertain (-3% to -5% across reports).

positions.thesis: Cigna at ~$271 is ~8.9x its raised 2026 adjusted EPS guide (>= $30.60) after a ~8% drop from $294 on Nov 17. That drop was sympathy selling on CMS's CRUSH Medicare Advantage RADV proposal, but CI exited MA/Part D when it sold the business to HCSC in March 2025, so the rule barely touches its earnings. Evernorth/commercial earnings plus heavy buybacks justify upsizing to the book's largest weight on mispriced regulatory contagion. An 18% stop sits below the March 12-month low area of ~$258.

CVS is still statistically cheap (low-teens P/E, ~3.5% yield, Aetna margin repair underway). Aetna's Medicare Advantage book is directly exposed to the proposed CRUSH RADV audit regime and a soft 2027 rate backdrop, though, so the risk/reward is worse than CI's. I am trimming it to a 7% residual: I keep the value exposure if the proposal is softened in comment, and I reduce the damage if it is finalized as written. The existing 20% stop is kept.

Citigroup is the cheapest money-center bank at ~1.3x book. The restructuring/expense program and buybacks are intact, and the week's selloff is AI-led rather than a credit event: Treasury yields eased and there is no sign of funding stress. Size is unchanged and the 20% stop is held, since it is still -8.6% on the leg and inside the stop.

Pfizer is a high-yield, single-digit-multiple large-cap pharma with low beta to the AI unwind and no Medicare Advantage exposure. It is the book's defensive ballast through the drawdown. Size and stop are unchanged.

Chevron is an FCF-rich integrated major with dividend plus buyback. Brent near $92 is still elevated despite the ~20% November slide on rising Mideast exports, and renewed US-Iran fighting and tanker attacks near Hormuz keep the tail-risk hedge relevant. The leg is -6.4% and inside its 15% stop. Size is unchanged.

Exxon is the second leg of the Brent/Hormuz stub, with low-cost Guyana/Permian supply and a strong balance sheet. It is -9.7% on the leg and inside its 15% stop. I keep it at 8% rather than adding, because the IEA sees a Q4 supply surplus that caps upside outside a Hormuz disruption.
Bristol-Myers is a single-digit-P/E pharma with a high dividend. It has been flat on the leg through an 8.6% SPY drawdown week, which shows its defensive role. Size and stop are unchanged.
